title: Do We Owe Future People?
objective: After this level you can explain why duties to people not yet born are puzzling, including Parfit’s non-identity problem, and apply it to a long-term choice.
summary: A different choice brings different people into existence, so Parfit’s depletion case seems to harm no one yet seems wrong; replies disagree.

cards.headline: Can you harm someone whose very existence depends on your choice?
cards.body: It sounds like a riddle. Derek Parfit showed it is a real problem for any choice that reaches far into the future.

cards.headline: You almost weren’t
cards.body: Had your parents delayed having a child by a few months, the odds are that a different person would exist instead of you. Gregory Kavka called this the precariousness of existence. Derek Parfit, in his 1984 book Reasons and Persons, saw that it turns long-term choices into a puzzle.

cards.headline: Depletion
cards.body: Parfit’s case: a community chooses to deplete a resource rather than conserve it. For two centuries life is slightly better; after that, much lower. But the choice also changes who gets conceived, so the later people would never have existed under conservation. If their lives are still worth living, depletion seems to make none of them worse off.

cards.headline: Bad for whom?
cards.body: The trouble is a natural idea Parfit summed up as “what is bad must be bad for someone”. Combined with depletion, it implies the choice harms no one. Yet Parfit held that the great lowering of the quality of life must give some moral reason not to choose it. That clash is the non-identity problem.

mascot.line: Don’t memorize the dates. Remember the move: change the choice, change who exists.

cards.headline: Ways out
cards.body: Some philosophers, such as David Boonin, bite the bullet: such choices are not wrong after all. Others drop the idea that bad must be bad for someone and judge outcomes impersonally, as total utilitarianism does, by adding up well-being whoever has it. None of the replies has won the field; it remains among the most challenging problems in population ethics.

cards.headline: Do We Owe Future People?: the big picture
learned: “What is bad must be bad for someone”
Replies: bite the bullet, or go impersonal

questions.prompt: How did Parfit sum up the person-affecting idea behind the non-identity problem?

options.label: “The needs of the many outweigh the few”
“What is bad must be bad for someone”
“Only present people count”
options.rationale: That is not the idea he named.

questions.explanation: Parfit summed it up as “what is bad must be bad for someone”.

questions.prompt: A country picks a cheap energy plan that will lower the quality of life two centuries from now, for people who would not exist under the other plan. Why is it hard to say the plan harms them?

options.label: The harm is too small and too distant to measure
Future people cannot have any interests of their own
Without the plan, those people would never have existed
The plan will surely be reversed long before then
options.rationale: Nothing in the case says so.

questions.explanation: The plan changes who is conceived; if the people it affects have lives worth living, it seems to make none of them worse off than they would otherwise have been.

questions.prompt: Parfit’s puzzle rests on a biological fact: a different time of conception means a different person. What does Level 1 say about philosophers and such findings?

options.label: They replace arguments with experiments
options.rationale: The argument is still where the work happens.

options.label: They wait for science to settle the moral question
They often use them as premises

questions.explanation: Level 1 notes that philosophers often use scientific findings as premises, as Parfit does with the precariousness of existence.
